steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A crime requires two elements: actus reus (the guilty act) and mens rea (the guilty mind)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Actus reus can be a positive act, a failure to act (omission) or a state of affairs

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Omissions generally do not create criminal liability unless there is a duty to act (e.g. parent–child, contract)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Causation requires both factual causation ('but for' test) and legal causation (proximate cause)

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the difference between actus reus and mens rea? | Q: When can an omission form the actus reus of a crime? | Q: What is the 'but for' test in causation?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Actus reus is the physical element (the guilty act, omission or state of affairs); mens rea is the mental element (the guilty mind, such as intention or recklessness). Both must be present for most cr | An omission can be actus reus only where there is a legal duty to act — for example, a parent's duty to care for a child, a contractual duty (e.g. a lifeguard), or a duty arising from having created a | The factual causation test: would the result have happened 'but for' the defendant's act? If the answer is no, the defendant is a factual cause of the result.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always discuss both actus reus and mens rea when analysing criminal liability Omissions are a favourite exam topic — know the situations where a duty to act arises Causation questions require you to apply both the 'but for' test and legal causation Strict liability is often tested — know examples and be able to evaluate arguments for and against Explain the difference between direct and oblique intention using case examples
